content: Poor outcomes following breech birth may result from underlying conditions that lead to breech presentation or from factors associated with the delivery process itself. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of planned caesarean section for singleton breech presentation at term on various pregnancy outcomes. The review included three randomized trials involving 2,396 participants. Among women assigned to a vaginal delivery protocol, 45% ultimately underwent caesarean delivery, compared to 91% of women assigned to planned caesarean section. The evidence for this finding was graded as low quality. Planned caesarean section was associated with a reduction in perinatal or neonatal death (excluding fatal anomalies) or severe neonatal morbidity in countries with low national perinatal mortality rates. Specifically, the risk ratio (RR) was 0.07 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.02 to 0.29) in one study involving 1,025 women, with evidence graded as moderate quality. However, this benefit was not observed in countries with high national perinatal mortality rates (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.24, one study, 1,053 women, low-quality evidence). The difference between these subgroups was statistically significant, with substantial heterogeneity noted. A random-effects analysis showed that the overall effect was not statistically significant (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.02 to 2.44, one study, 2,078 infants). Planned caesarean section reduced the risk of perinatal or neonatal death (excluding fatal anomalies) across all settings (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.86, three studies, 2,388 women). However, the sample sizes were insufficient to conclusively determine reductions in birth trauma or brachial plexus injury. Neither outcome reached statistical significance. For birth trauma, the RR was 0.42 (95% CI 0.16 to 1.10, one study, 2,062 infants, low-quality evidence), and for brachial plexus injury, the RR was 0.35 (95% CI 0.08 to 1.47, three studies, 2,375 infants, low-quality evidence). Planned caesarean section was associated with a modest increase in short-term maternal morbidity (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.61, three studies, 2,396 women, low-quality evidence). At three months postpartum, women in the planned caesarean section group reported less urinary incontinence (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.93, one study, 1,595 women), no significant difference in overall pain (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.29, one study, 1,593 women, low-quality evidence), more abdominal pain (RR 1.89, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.79, one study, 1,593 women), and less perineal pain (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.58, one study, 1,593 women). At two years postpartum, there were no significant differences in the combined outcome of death or neurodevelopmental delay (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.52 to 2.30, one study, 920 children, low-quality evidence). However, more infants in the planned caesarean section group had medical problems at two years (RR 1.41, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.89, one study, 843 children). Maternal outcomes at two years were similar between groups. In countries with low perinatal mortality rates, planned caesarean section was associated with lower healthcare costs, with a mean difference of -$877.00 (95% CI -$894.89 to -$859.11, one study, 1,027 women, expressed in 2002 Canadian dollars). The trials included in this review had several design limitations, and the overall quality of evidence was graded as low. None of the studies blinded the intervention, and two trials had suboptimal random allocation processes. Two of the three trials had serious design flaws, but these contributed fewer outcomes compared to a larger, multi-center trial with a lower risk of bias. In conclusion, planned caesarean section for term breech presentation reduced perinatal or neonatal death and the composite outcome of death or serious neonatal morbidity, albeit with a slight increase in maternal morbidity. At two years, there was an increase in infant medical problems following planned caesarean section, but no significant difference in long-term neurodevelopmental delay or the combined outcome of death or neurodevelopmental delay. The findings highlight the need to balance the benefits of planned caesarean section against maternal preferences, potential risks in future pregnancies, and the specific healthcare context. Further research is needed to improve the safety of breech delivery and to explore the potential association between caesarean section and infant medical problems. These findings are not generalizable to settings where caesarean section is not readily available or to delivery methods that differ significantly from those used in the reviewed trials.
